0c1160d31848.headline: Moon Spuds Pass the Taste-Safety Test: Potatoes Grown in Fake Lunar Soil Are Safe to Eat
body: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil are safe to eat, according to a new study from Oregon State University in the US, reported by Metro. The research, published in the journal npj Microgravity, suggests the humble spud could be a serious contender for future lunar menus.

The team, led by Professor Aymeric Goyer of the university's College of Agricultural Sciences and backed by Nasa funding, planted potatoes in lunar regolith simulants. Regolith is the loose rock and dust covering most of the moon's surface, and it contains very little organic matter. The researchers mixed in different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich amendment made by using earthworms to break down organic material.

The amount mattered. Plants grown in simulants with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those raised in Earth soil. Plants with no amendment were described as severely impaired, with stunting and underdeveloped roots, while those with 5% to 15% vermicompost recovered only partially.

Because moon dirt differs from place to place, the team tested five simulants representing both lunar mare and highland regions. They also grew potatoes in soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for the highest potato yields in the world, as an Earth benchmark.

Safety was the other big question. Lunar regolith contains elevated levels of heavy metals, but the researchers believe organic matter helps by binding them, reducing damage to roots and growth. They found no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, the natural potato toxins often linked to green discolouration under the skin.

The findings fit Nasa's Artemis goal of a sustained human presence on the moon, which would be far easier if food were produced there rather than shipped from Earth at great cost. The researchers say astronauts could carry a small amount of organic matter and then make more by converting food scraps and plant waste. Potatoes were chosen because they yield more calories per unit of land than many crops and are considered a practical staple for long missions.
0c1160d31848.summary: Oregon State University researchers found potatoes grown in simulated moon soil enriched with vermicompost matched Earth-grown plants and showed no significant rise in toxins, a step toward growing food for long lunar missions.
0c1160d31848.pixel_take: The Martian proved potatoes can survive on another world. Now science says the moon version won't poison you. Mash, boil, stick them in a lunar stew: the space race just got carb-loaded.
0c1160d31848.why_it_matters: Resupplying a lunar base from Earth is hugely expensive, so any way to grow food on site could cut mission costs. That matters for the commercial and government space sector, and for anyone watching the economics of long-term space exploration.
key_points: Potatoes in simulated lunar soil with 30% vermicompost grew as well as in Earth soil.
No statistically significant rise in glycoalkaloid toxins was found, despite heavy metals in regolith.

9329f8e154dd.headline: Big Bao Swallows Little Bao in a Cosmic Pac-Man Merger Near Andromeda
body: Astronomers have caught a giant star eating its smaller companion on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, according to a new paper in the journal Nature. The merged star has been nicknamed Bao, and it may have been effectively rejuvenated by the meal.

The victim, dubbed Little Bao, had about 0.7 times the mass of the Sun. Its host, Big Bao, was a supergiant roughly seven times the Sun's mass, with a radius 350 times larger and a brightness about 18,000 times greater. Lead author Viraj Karambelkar's team says the pair had orbited each other for thousands of years before the collision.

What makes this special is the timing. Stellar mergers are hard to predict, so they are rarely seen live. The team flagged something odd in February 2023, using data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. Later telescopes tracked the star brightening and shedding dust, and the Zwicky Transient Facility recorded the eruption on 17 October 2025.

The James Webb Space Telescope then observed Bao on 24 December 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. The researchers say that is the earliest follow-up of an event like this. Webb's mid-infrared data revealed the dust the larger star had released over hundreds of years.

The merger also moved fast. Once Little Bao touched the giant's surface, it took only seven orbits, about seven years, to finish the job. Other known mergers involving smaller stars have taken thousands of orbits. Co-author Kishalay De described it as almost like a bomb going off inside a living star.

The process is called common envelope evolution. Sometimes both stars survive and later become neutron stars, black holes, supernovae, gravitational-wave sources or millisecond pulsars. Here, simulations showed Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Scientists say more observations are needed to pin down Bao's final properties.
9329f8e154dd.summary: Astronomers watched a supergiant star swallow a smaller companion near Andromeda, with the James Webb Space Telescope capturing the aftermath just 47 days after the eruption peaked, according to a new Nature paper.
9329f8e154dd.pixel_take: Little Bao went from binary partner to main course in seven years. Somewhere, a very patient supergiant is still chewing, and astronomers are taking notes.
9329f8e154dd.why_it_matters: Rapid-response space observation is a growing field, and this event shows how coordinated telescope networks and fast data pipelines can catch fleeting events. Better models of stellar mergers also feed into understanding black holes and gravitational waves, which drive long-term science and tech investment.
key_points: A supergiant about 7 times the Sun's mass swallowed a 0.7-solar-mass companion near Andromeda.
Webb observed the merged star, Bao, just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest such follow-up.
The merger took about seven years, far faster than other known mergers involving smaller stars.

aa820a7101e6.headline: Married 58 Years and Sharing One Wallet: Why Do So Many Couples Split Their Money?
body: A reader writing to MarketWatch's money advice column says he has been married for 58 years and has always treated the household finances as "our" money, not "his" and "hers." The question he raises is why so many couples today keep their finances separate.

According to the teaser, his wife stopped working outside the home in 1970. That detail frames his view: in his marriage, one partner's paycheck was the family's paycheck, and the idea of dividing it into separate accounts never came up. The full text of the column was not available to us, so we can't report what answer, if any, the columnist gave.

The question still points to a real debate in personal finance. Some couples pool everything into joint accounts, others keep separate accounts, and many land on a hybrid, with a shared account for bills and individual accounts for personal spending. Each setup has its fans, and each can work when both partners are open about it.

Money is also one of the most common sources of tension in relationships, and secrecy tends to make it worse. Whether accounts are joint or separate, the habit that matters most is knowing where the household stands: what is owed, what is saved and what the plan is for retirement.

The letter also shows how much has changed in six decades. Arrangements where one spouse works outside the home and the other manages the household were common in 1970. Today, two-income households are far more common, and many partners arrive with their own savings, debts and financial habits, which makes separate accounts feel natural to some.

7959f46d944f.headline: Passenger sues driver over chicken-induced braking, loses and is ordered to pay costs
body: A woman in Singapore who sued her private-hire driver after he braked hard to avoid a car that had stopped for a chicken has lost her case. According to Metro, citing CNA, she was ordered to pay S$15,000 (about £8,700) in legal costs.

The incident happened on February 19, 2024, on Holland Road. Ms Yvonne Chen Qianyun was a passenger in a car driven by Mr Tan Teng Kiat. A chicken wandered in front of the vehicle ahead, which braked, and Mr Tan then braked too to avoid hitting it.

Ms Chen, whose injuries were not specified in the judgment, sued for negligence. She argued he had not left enough space and had stopped more forcefully than needed. Mr Tan said he was driving at around 50km/h, about 10 metres behind the other car, and had enough room and time to stop safely.

He also told the court that Ms Chen had first asked whether he had noted the number plate of the car in front, because she wanted to pursue that driver over her worsening back pain. He said she even asked him to be a witness, before later deciding to sue him instead.

Judge Ng noted that Ms Chen had at least two other cases pending in the district court, both over separate road accidents: one in September 2022 involving a private-hire car, and one in October 2024 involving her husband's car. She was a passenger in both.

The judge accepted she was an innocent passenger, but said the driver was not to blame. The law, the judge said, does not look for someone at fault for every loss, and some losses must lie where they fall. The chicken crossing was, in the judge's words, part of the 'vicissitudes of life'.

332891161480.headline: Wood from Turkey's 'Noah's Ark' site dates to about 4,300 years old, but the boat-shaped hill stays a hill for now
body: Researchers studying the Durupınar Formation in Turkey's Ağrı Province, a boat-shaped site long linked by some believers to Noah's Ark, say wood samples from the site date to roughly 4,300 years ago, according to Metro, citing Turkey's İhlas News Agency.

Prof Cenker Atilla of Sivas Cumhuriyet University confirmed on Sunday that the team had received first results from a US laboratory. They place the samples between 2400 and 2200 BC. The material, described as wood and carbonised matter, was collected in late summer near the village of Üzengili in the Doğubayazıt district.

Andrew Jones, deputy leader of the team, said two wood samples gave dates of about 4,300 years. He noted that this lines up with some proposed chronologies of the biblical flood. He also acknowledged that the findings alone do not prove the formation is the Ark.

That caveat matters. Radiocarbon dating estimates age by measuring the carbon-14 left in organic material. It says nothing about how the wood was used, whether humans shaped it, or how it ended up buried there. Answering those questions means studying the samples' physical traits and the geological deposits around them.

The team is now waiting on independent results from laboratories in Switzerland and from facilities linked to TÜBİTAK, Türkiye's science and technology research council. Earlier geological studies concluded the formation was created by natural processes, and the new dates do not overturn that conclusion or link the wood to an ancient vessel.
332891161480.summary: Wood samples from Turkey's Durupınar Formation, long tied to Noah's Ark, date to about 4,300 years old. Researchers admit that doesn't prove it's the Ark, and more lab results are pending.

21618591f957.headline: Georgia donkey swishes back into record books with world's longest tail
body: A donkey in Georgia has landed a new Guinness World Record, this time for the longest tail on a donkey, according to UPI. The certified length is 19.97 inches, which is just shy of 20 inches and presumably a source of quiet agony for anyone who likes round numbers.

Quirky Guinness titles like this tend to travel far on social media, and UPI notes the story came with video. For owners and small farms, a record can mean a burst of attention that no advertising budget could easily buy, which is a lesson in niche branding if there ever was one.

62d977b7d482.headline: Poundland falls into administration, putting 11,000 jobs on the line weeks before Christmas
body: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its US owners Gordon Brothers failed to secure a buyer for the discount chain, according to BBC News. Shops and distribution centres will keep trading for now, though the business is likely to be broken up and some stores sold to rivals.

Alix Partners has been appointed administrator and says it will weigh all options, including selling the business or its assets in whole or in part. Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff the board had "no alternative", saying Gordon Brothers removed borrowing facilities and access to bank accounts on 27 October and did not release enough funds afterwards to keep the company solvent.

Gordon Brothers rejected that picture. It says it explored every avenue to sell the whole company, loaned Poundland £85m over a year, and stepped in during 2025 when no one else would finance the business. It also said the retailer remained vulnerable to inflation and weaker sales or margins. The union Usdaw, which represents many staff, claimed the owner's intention was to force administration, a characterisation Gordon Brothers disputed.

A key sticking point was a shareholder loan the firm inherited when it bought Poundland for less than £1 last year. Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m and previous owner Pepco £7.5m. Offers that would have kept the chain intact reportedly included Martin Property Group paying £5m upfront with the rest deferred to 2030, and Xyra offering £12.5m upfront but running out of time. Zachert Private Equity is understood to have made a late bid.

Politics is piling in. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the news deeply concerning but said administration lets other buyers engage. Labour MP Liam Byrne said the Commons business committee will recall Gordon Brothers, and wants to know how much money is being taken out. Critics allege the firm could profit from selling the 600 shops and stock piecemeal; Gordon Brothers denies this.

Meanwhile, restricted funds meant shelves were not being restocked fast enough ahead of the festive season. For staff such as 62-year-old Kelvin Blake, 25 years at the firm, the worry is whether new jobs will be there.
62d977b7d482.summary: Poundland has entered administration after owner Gordon Brothers failed to find a buyer, putting 11,000 jobs at risk. Stores keep trading while administrators weigh a sale, and MPs plan to question the owner.
62d977b7d482.why_it_matters: The collapse of a major high street discounter threatens thousands of jobs just before Christmas and could reshape the cut-price retail market as rivals pick over its stores. It also raises questions about how distressed-debt investors handle struggling retailers.
key_points: Poundland is in administration with 11,000 jobs at risk; stores keep trading for now.
Gordon Brothers and the company's board and union dispute who is to blame; the owner denies profiting from a break-up.
MPs will recall Gordon Brothers, while administrators Alix Partners consider selling the business whole or in parts.

86a17b54466b.headline: China's 'Female Gaze' Boom: Male Dancers and Hiking Hunks Cash In on Women's Fantasies
body: A growing entertainment industry in China is built around what is often called the "female gaze," according to The New York Times. The offerings range from male dancers to handsome hiking companions, all aimed at women as paying customers.

The Times describes the sector as thriving, and says it is testing the limits of what Beijing is willing to tolerate. The material available gives no figures on revenue, audience size or specific companies, so the scale of the boom is not quantified here.

The pattern is a familiar one in consumer economics. When a large group of customers finds that existing products were designed with someone else in mind, entrepreneurs notice, and a new market takes shape. Entertainment aimed at women's tastes, rather than at men's, is the latest example of that dynamic in China.

The tension with authorities is the interesting part. China's government regulates entertainment and public culture closely, and any business built on fantasy and desire has to work out where the line sits. According to the Times, that line is being probed, though the teaser does not say how officials have responded.
For now, the story is a snapshot of a market finding its footing: demand is visible, the supply is inventive, and the rulebook is still being read in real time.

27d0f525dd6c.headline: Brazil Says 'Unacceptable,' China Cries 'Manipulation' as Trump Proposes Tariffs on 14 Partners
body: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, Vietnam and Brazil, drawing sharp rebukes from several capitals on Wednesday, according to The Guardian.

Brazil was the loudest. Its government said it "will not yield to this type of threat" and called the move unacceptable while bilateral talks are still under way. It singled out higher duties on raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, which would hit Embraer, its largest aircraft maker. Brazil said it would keep negotiating but did not rule out retaliation. Washington singled Brazil out after talks stalled.

The tariffs rest on a law that lets the president target countries found to use unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. US trade representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that many partners use market-distorting practices that erode America's manufacturing base. Rates would be capped at levels agreed in existing or pending trade deals. The administration will seek industry feedback and hold a hearing on 25 January, which suggests final duties would not bite until February or March.

China faces potentially the biggest hit: a capped rate of 20%, which in some cases stacks with other levies to reach 45%. Beijing's embassy said the "industrial overcapacity" issue does not really exist and should not be a pretext for political manipulation, though it stopped short of threatening retaliation. Greer said a broad exemption is proposed for $30bn of Chinese goods in line with last year's truce, which expires on 10 January 2027. Analyst Derek Scissors of the American Enterprise Institute argued the proposal barely raises existing tariffs and will not change China's behavior.

Others responded with varying degrees of irritation. The EU said it rejects the premise and expects the US to honor last year's deal. Japan called the move regrettable, Singapore said it was very disappointed, and India denied having excess capacity, noting its rate would be capped at 17% if a deal is struck. Vietnam is preparing rebuttal comments, and Taiwan expects to keep its 15% rate.

At home, the tariffs may prove durable. Some Democrats could back levies on China, and Trump can veto any bill to overturn them. Still, Senator Ron Wyden, who will lead the finance committee next year, vowed to use every tool to end what he called tariff chaos.
27d0f525dd6c.summary: Trump's administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the EU and Brazil. Brazil called it unacceptable and China called it political manipulation, while final duties are unlikely before February or March.
27d0f525dd6c.pixel_take: Washington hands out 14 tariff proposals with a hearing date attached. It's less a trade war than a trade war with a public comment period.
27d0f525dd6c.why_it_matters: Tariffs on goods from major partners can raise import prices and ripple through supply chains, affecting companies and consumers. Capped rates tied to existing deals suggest negotiation leverage more than a total reset, but retaliation threats keep markets and exporters on edge.
key_points: The US proposed tariffs on 14 partners, with a hearing on 25 January and final duties likely in February or March.
Brazil objects to sugar and 10% aircraft tariffs and keeps retaliation open; China faces a capped 20% rate, up to 45% stacked.
Rates would be capped at levels in existing or pending trade deals, and the EU, Japan, India and others pushed back.

0279088714aa.headline: Two Best Friends Climb an Ecuador Mountain to Play Chess at 20,593 Feet, Setting a Record
body: Two American best friends have taken the phrase "high-level play" literally. According to UPI, the pair climbed an Ecuador mountain to an altitude of 20,593 feet and played a game of chess there that earned a Guinness World Record.

The material available gives the headline facts: the climbers are two men from the United States, they are close friends, the mountain is in Ecuador, and the altitude reached was 20,593 feet. The game itself counts as a record-breaking one, according to the report.
Details such as the date of the climb, the mountain's name, who won the game and the exact record category were not included in the material we received, so we will not guess at them.

Still, the stunt makes sense as part of a long tradition of people taking ordinary pastimes to extreme places. Chess needs only a board, pieces and two stubborn minds, which makes it surprisingly portable. At that height, though, the air holds far less oxygen than at sea level, and clear thinking is exactly what thin air tends to erode. Playing a full game there is as much an endurance test as a mental one.
Record attempts like this also say something about modern attention economics: a niche board game becomes international news when it is attached to a mountain and a Guinness certificate.
0279088714aa.summary: Two American best friends climbed a mountain in Ecuador to 20,593 feet and played a chess game that earned a Guinness World Record, UPI reports.

0e4e290de456.headline: Cat Wedged in Virginia Drainpipe Needs Fire Department Rescue, Looks Deeply Unimpressed
body: A young tabby cat got itself stuck in a drainpipe beneath a street in Richmond, Virginia, in the US, and needed a multi-team rescue to get out, according to Metro.

Photos show the cat peering out of a small circular opening in the ground, wearing what Metro described as an unimpressed expression. A scattering of cat treats sat tantalisingly close by, though the treats alone were not enough to solve the problem.
Animal control officers called in the local fire department for help. Crews spent time hammering, cutting and digging to open up a space large enough to reach the animal.

Richmond Animal Care and Control said the rescue was a true team effort involving a lot of hammering, cutting, pulling, digging and problem-solving. The agency added that every team worked together efficiently and safely.
Eventually a firefighter was able to reach inside and lift the cat to safety. The tabby came out uninjured, with its nine lives apparently still intact, per Metro.

8832ade22747.headline: Stray Las Vegas pit bull tips the scales at 137 pounds, and rescuers now have a diet plan
body: A stray pit bull found in Las Vegas weighed in at 137 pounds, and animal rescuers are now putting together a weight loss plan for the dog, according to UPI.

For context, 137 pounds is far above what is typical for the breed. Vets commonly recommend that overweight dogs lose weight gradually, under professional guidance, with controlled portions and gentle exercise rather than crash diets.

Stories like this also show the less visible work shelters and rescues do. Taking in a stray is only the first step, and a dog that needs a specialized care plan can mean extra vet visits, special food and more staff time, all of which cost money. 7c98b739ab03.headline: XPeng's IRON humanoid robot is aiming for an EV-sized price tag and a 2027 launch
body: Chinese EV maker XPeng says its IRON humanoid robot could cost roughly as much as an electric vehicle when it goes on sale to the public in 2027, according to Digital Trends. The company showed off the latest version at its AI Day, where the robot answered audience questions live on stage.

XPeng Vice Chairman Brian Gu told Bloomberg that the price could sit around the median selling price of an EV, though he gave no exact figure. IRON is due to start training as a retail assistant in XPeng stores in the first quarter of 2027, with a public launch planned for the second quarter. The company is targeting sales of tens of thousands of units that year.

On paper, IRON is more than a walking mannequin. It has 76 degrees of freedom, more than 1,500 tactile sensing points and three in-house Turing AI chips running its onboard models and whole-body control. XPeng says it can navigate on its own, take tasks by voice or app, recharge itself and keep tabs on its own health.

Your living room will have to wait. XPeng plans to start in commercial settings, move to industrial uses and only later reach homes. Gu suggested household deployment could follow one to two years after commercial success, with safety around children, elderly people and pets among the hurdles.

There is also a business model beyond the hardware. XPeng sees potential recurring revenue from software subscriptions, upgrades, training and services. So the robot may come with its own version of the gadget subscription habit, on top of a car-sized price tag.
7c98b739ab03.summary: XPeng says its IRON humanoid robot could cost about as much as a typical EV when it launches in 2027. Stores come first, homes later, and subscriptions may follow.
7c98b739ab03.pixel_take: A robot priced like a car, with subscriptions on top. Finally, a way to pay monthly fees for something that might fold your laundry.
7c98b739ab03.why_it_matters: A humanoid robot at EV prices tests whether consumers and businesses will pay car money for general-purpose machines. XPeng's plan for recurring software and service revenue shows where robotics makers hope the profits will come from. 2027 sales will show if humanoids are moving beyond demos.
key_points: IRON is targeted at roughly the median EV selling price, with a public launch in Q2 2027.
It trains as a retail assistant in XPeng stores from Q1 2027, with tens of thousands of units targeted.
Homes come last, one to two years after commercial use, with subscriptions eyed for recurring revenue.

11e0cf03506c.headline: Georgia judge hits pause on her own order to hand over 2020 ballot copies
body: A judge in Fulton County, Georgia, has blocked her own order requiring that electronic copies of 2020 election ballots be turned over to the state election board, according to The Guardian. Superior court judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

The order concerned electronic copies of ballots from the 2020 election that the FBI had seized. The material was to go to the state board, but the county's appeal has now frozen that handover while the dispute moves forward.

The source material available is brief, so the details behind the seizure, the board's reasons for wanting the copies and the county's grounds for appeal are not laid out here. What is clear is the sequence: an order was issued, county officials challenged it, and the same judge stepped in to stop it from taking effect.

Pausing an order once an appeal is filed is a common procedural move. It keeps the status quo in place so that a higher court can review the matter before anything irreversible happens, and in this case it means the ballot copies stay where they are for now.

The episode shows that fights over the 2020 vote in Georgia are still being litigated years later, with election officials, state authorities and federal investigators all in the mix. Further rulings from the appeals process will determine whether and when the state board gets the copies.
11e0cf03506c.summary: A Fulton County judge paused her own order to give the state election board electronic copies of 2020 ballots seized by the FBI, after county election officials filed a notice of appeal, The Guardian reports.
11e0cf03506c.pixel_take: The judge has issued an order, then stopped it herself. It's the legal version of hitting 'undo send' while the county's lawyers are already on the phone with the appeals court.
11e0cf03506c.why_it_matters: Lingering disputes over how 2020 election records are handled keep election administration in Georgia in legal limbo, which matters for public trust and for how future elections are run. Prolonged litigation also costs counties and taxpayers money and keeps political risk in the headlines.
key_points: Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused her own order on 2020 ballot copies.
The copies were seized by the FBI and were to go to the state board.

a1e1f2b8b606.headline: Trump's New Tariffs Arrive With Less Fanfare, and the World Is Already Looking Past Him
body: The latest round of Trump tariffs, announced this week, is landing far more quietly than last April's, according to BBC News economics editor Faisal Islam. There was no Rose Garden reveal, no gameshow-style board and no "Liberation Day" rhetoric. Instead, the mood is tentative, with talk of further negotiations.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC he expects a broad, even plurilateral, negotiation on excess capacity. The tariffs are not due to take effect until January or possibly February, after a consultation period, and the announced rates are upper ceilings that can be bargained down. Around the world, the BBC reports, the move is seen as an effort to shore up the legal footing of the tariffs rather than a real shift in strategy.

That footing matters because the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. For many countries there are now two legal bases: the new argument that foreign industrial support harms US goods trade, and the older forced labour provisions. The UK was unaffected by the new announcements but remains subject to an extra 10% under the forced labour rules. A group of 25 states is suing to strike those tariffs down.

Politics may matter as much as law. The tariffs must be finalised under a Democrat-controlled Congress, which has influence but not outright power. Incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said the new House would move to repeal them in its first 100 days. Over half of the Canada tariffs rest on a 1930s Smoot-Hawley provision, and a Senate bill to repeal them already exists. Enough rebel Republicans could threaten to override a veto.

China's rate of 20% is the truce level from last year's Trump-Xi deal, which expires in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, calling overcapacity a "false issue". Its leverage has grown: the US share of Chinese exports has fallen to about 10%, from 19% in 2018. China's 2026 exports to the US are down about 8% on 2024, yet gains elsewhere more than 25 times offset that.

Canada's exports to the US are flat, while its sales to the rest of the world have surged. With next month's G20 summit at Trump's Miami resort ahead, the open question is how much of the America First trade agenda Democrats will keep. Economists expect some tariffs to last for years.
a1e1f2b8b606.summary: Trump's new tariffs come with little fanfare, delayed start dates and negotiable ceilings, says the BBC. Trade has rerouted around the US, and Democrats in Congress may soon challenge the tariffs.
a1e1f2b8b606.pixel_take: Last April came with a gameshow board; this time the tariffs tiptoe in like a guest who knows the host may be evicted by Congress. Even trade wars, it seems, get tired.
a1e1f2b8b606.why_it_matters: Tariffs that are legally shaky, negotiable and politically contested make planning harder for businesses and investors. If the rest of the world keeps rerouting trade, US tariff leverage fades, while some duties may still linger for years and keep pressure on prices.
key_points: New tariffs are upper ceilings, start in January or February, and are open to negotiation.
China and Canada have rerouted exports to other markets, softening the impact.
A Democrat Congress and court challenges threaten the tariffs' long-term survival.

b2806a3d9fe8.headline: FedEx Jet Overshoots Runway at Miami Airport, Snarling Flights but Sparing Crew
body: A FedEx plane overran a runway after landing at Miami International Airport on Wednesday and came to a stop near a fence, according to The New York Times. The incident disrupted flights at the busy Florida hub.

Investigations into the cause generally follow, though the source material does not say who is looking into this one.

Miami International is a major gateway for both passengers and cargo, so even a short interruption can mean delays and rerouted flights. For a cargo carrier like FedEx, the timing matters too, since Wednesday fell in the heavy holiday shipping season. The article does not say whether any deliveries were affected.
For now, the headline fact is the good one: a plane ended up beside a fence rather than in a far worse place, and nobody was reported hurt.

0adfc9d68551.headline: Amazon Workers in 20-Plus Countries Plan Black Friday and Cyber Monday Strikes and Protests
body: Amazon workers and their supporters plan strikes and protests in more than 20 countries around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, according to Engadget. Trade union federation UNI Global says the aim is to push Amazon to negotiate with unions and respect employees' right to organize.

In the US, Teamsters plan Cyber Monday (November 30) protests in Los Angeles and Chicago. A local Teamsters union in Southern California said workers are demanding fair wages, safer conditions, union recognition and respect on the job.

In Germany, the union Verdi called strikes at 11 Amazon sites on Black Friday (November 27). It says pay often falls short of a living wage and that warehouse work puts considerable physical strain on staff. Per Deutsche Presse-Agentur, Verdi also claims Amazon uses digital trackers to monitor around 40,000 employees. An Amazon spokesman denied the claims and said average starting pay is above the German minimum wage.

Action is also planned in countries including Canada, Australia, India, Bangladesh, Poland, Brazil, Japan, South Africa and others. UNI Global says this is the seventh year of the Make Amazon Pay campaign, which it convenes with Progressive International.

The timing follows recent legal milestones. Earlier this month, workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, became the first in North America to win a union contract with Amazon, though its three-year terms were imposed through binding arbitration. It includes raises of up to $29 CAD per hour, an extra week of vacation after 10 years and up to 18 weeks of severance. Amazon called the process improper and unfair and said it may go to court.

In the US, the NLRB ordered Amazon in April to recognize and bargain with a union at the JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island, New York, which voted to unionize in 2022. Amazon is contesting that order. Engadget says it has contacted Amazon for comment.
0adfc9d68551.summary: Workers in more than 20 countries plan strikes and protests around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, demanding Amazon bargain with unions. Amazon disputes some union claims, per Engadget.
0adfc9d68551.pixel_take: Black Friday is when Amazon's machine runs hottest, so workers picked the day the gears are most visible. Nothing says 'please hear us' like doing it during the biggest sales weekend.
0adfc9d68551.why_it_matters: Black Friday and Cyber Monday are peak retail days, so labor action then gets attention, even if delivery impact is unclear. Ongoing fights over union recognition and arbitration could shape labor costs and working conditions at one of the world's largest employers.
key_points: Workers in 20+ countries plan strikes and protests on Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Verdi called strikes at 11 German sites; Teamsters plan protests in Los Angeles and Chicago.
Amazon denies Verdi's pay claims and is contesting union rulings in Canada and the US.

7fb91d3ccc37.headline: Yorkshire animal communicator says pets spill secrets, and ginger cats are brutal fashion critics
body: Emma Dawn, a 45-year-old former hairdresser from East Riding, Yorkshire, says she can talk to animals and relay what they really think of their owners, according to Metro. Her verdict on the feline fashion police: ginger cats are the rudest of all.

Dawn says she switched careers after being impressed by a professional pet communicator who spoke to her own dogs. She describes herself as a medium who quiets her conscious mind and receives messages mostly as pictures and short videos. She also says she can feel an animal's symptoms and pinpoint where it hurts, and that vets have told her the diagnoses are usually correct.

Dogs, she says, are the worst at spilling secrets, from owners sneaking food while dieting to who has visited the house. Cats are the most mischievous and slowest to trust. She recalls one that answered every question with the opposite of the truth to make her look wrong, and another that told its owner to change their clothes because the colours did not suit their hair.

Rescue animals, she says, give the most vivid stories. One dog described being pulled from a hole full of snakes, which she says its owner confirmed. Another had survived on the streets and had once been stabbed, which helped explain why he disliked other dogs. Owners usually call her over behaviour changes, and she says causes can be mundane, like a rubbing harness or a dog missing a son who left for university.

Dawn aims for 45-minute sessions, asks the animal for proof only it and its owner would know, and says she never cuts off a pet in full flow. She admits some people think she invents it all to take their money, and says she cannot seem to connect with her own dogs.
7fb91d3ccc37.summary: A Yorkshire former hairdresser who calls herself an animal communicator told Metro that dogs betray owners' secrets and ginger cats deliver the rudest fashion critiques. Her claims are unproven, and she acknowledges some scepticism.
7fb91d3ccc37.pixel_take: Somewhere a ginger cat is reviewing your wardrobe and your midnight snacking. Honestly, a pet with opinions on your colour palette is still cheaper than a stylist.
7fb91d3ccc37.why_it_matters: The pet-care industry is a big consumer market, and owners spend freely on anything promising happier animals. Paid psychic readings are unregulated and the claims are not scientifically established, so check with a vet before paying for help with a health or behaviour problem.
key_points: Emma Dawn, 45, a former hairdresser from East Riding, says she talks to pets through images and feelings.
She says dogs reveal owners' secrets and ginger cats are the rudest.
She acknowledges sceptics who say she makes it up, and says she asks pets for proof before readings.

ed0e4cd4a390.headline: Auros, Hong Kong crypto market maker, is winding down operations
body: Auros, a Hong Kong-based crypto trading firm, is winding down its operations, according to CoinDesk. The report, published on November 26, 2026, gave no further details in the material available to us.

The news stands out because of the firm's size. Auros previously estimated that it handled about 4% of global crypto exchange trading volume, which is a large slice of a market that runs around the clock.

The firm also had fresh funding in recent memory. After the collapse of FTX, Auros raised $17 million, according to CoinDesk. That was a period when many crypto businesses were struggling to keep investors' confidence.

We don't know the reasons behind the wind-down, the timeline, or what it means for the firm's clients and staff, since those details were not in the material we received. We will not guess. Further reporting should clarify how orderly the exit will be.

For context, trading firms like this typically provide liquidity, meaning they quote prices so that others can buy and sell without moving the market too much. When a big player steps back, other firms usually fill the gap, though thinner liquidity can mean wider spreads for traders.
ed0e4cd4a390.summary: Hong Kong-based crypto trading firm Auros is winding down, CoinDesk reports. It once estimated it handled 4% of global exchange volume and raised $17 million after the FTX collapse.

4a8ad48b5c13.headline: ECB Taps Pablo Hernández de Cos to Succeed Lagarde, Who Is Heading for the Exit Early
body: The European Central Bank has chosen Pablo Hernández de Cos as its next president, according to The New York Times. The pick sets up a changing of the guard at the institution that steers monetary policy for the euro area.

The move follows the early departure of Christine Lagarde, who is leaving the presidency before her term runs out. The Times also reports that two vacancies are coming on the ECB's board, which means the leadership team in Frankfurt is about to look quite different.

The material available gives few further details, such as timing of the handover or the reasoning behind the selection, so those points remain to be confirmed. What is clear is that a president's exit combined with openings on the board creates a rare chance to reshape the institution's top ranks all at once.

For context, the ECB president chairs the Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the countries sharing the euro and acts as the public face of the bank. Markets watch every change at the top closely, because a new leader can bring a different tone on inflation, rates and crisis management, even when the institution's mandate stays the same.
Expect investors, bond traders and politicians across the euro area to spend the coming weeks reading the tea leaves on what the new leadership means for borrowing costs.

7a24f698eb93.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García lands in Spain, ending a 20-month fight that both sides now call a win
body: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran man wrongly deported to El Salvador last year, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday with his wife, according to The Guardian. His departure from the US closes a legal saga that lasted about 20 months and became a symbol of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

Both camps are claiming victory. Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said he had "self-deported" to Spain. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who had visited him in El Salvador, said he was relieved Ábrego García would be safe and free in a country of his choosing. A court order unsealed Wednesday shows the federal judge on the case had directed the administration to facilitate his voluntary departure and not interfere.

The back story, as The Guardian's analysis lays it out: he came to the US in 2011, lived in Maryland and held a work permit after a judge barred his removal to El Salvador over safety fears. In March 2025 he was deported there anyway, despite that protection. The administration later admitted an "administrative error", and after a court fight that reached the Supreme Court he was returned in June 2025.

Back in the US, he was charged with human smuggling over a 2022 traffic stop, and the government sought to send him to African countries. He offered Costa Rica, which the administration refused. In May a federal judge dismissed the smuggling case as a "vindictive prosecution". He has never been convicted of the other things officials called him publicly.

The Guardian's José Olivares argues that the administration still got what it wanted: a high-profile immigrant gone, and no one significantly held responsible for the deportation, the defiance of court orders or the alleged abuse at the Salvadoran prison where deportees were held. His lawyers hope a future president might let him return.
7a24f698eb93.summary: Kilmar Ábrego García, wrongly deported last year, has left the US for Spain. Both the Trump administration and his supporters claim victory, but The Guardian says accountability for the case remains scarce.
7a24f698eb93.why_it_matters: The case tested how far a government can go in ignoring court orders on deportation, a question that shapes the rule of law and the political climate around immigration policy. Enforcement fights like this also influence labor markets and business planning in sectors reliant on immigrant workers.
key_points: Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after a 20-month legal battle.
A judge had ordered the administration to facilitate his voluntary departure; both sides claim victory.
Critics say few officials have faced accountability for the wrongful deportation.

a3c3fc2706d7.headline: Judge Blocks Trump's Narrower Birthright Citizenship Order, Saying President Can't Carve Out New Exceptions
body: A US federal judge has struck down the Trump administration's latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship, according to Al Jazeera. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ruled on Wednesday that the US-born children covered by the new order are still subject to US jurisdiction and therefore guaranteed citizenship under the Constitution.

"The president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper wrote. A court in Maryland had already blocked the same policy with a preliminary injunction in September.

The order followed a June Supreme Court ruling that struck down Trump's first birthright citizenship order. The justices found that the drafters of the 14th Amendment knew how broad its language was and did not limit it the way the president wanted. The court cited an 1898 case involving Wong Kim Ark, a US-born Chinese American who was denied entry after returning from abroad.

Rather than give up, the administration issued a narrower set of orders in August. They targeted so-called birth tourism, children of foreign government or international organization workers who lack diplomatic immunity, and children with a parent classed as an alien enemy. Rights groups sued on behalf of affected children.

The ACLU's Cody Wofsy said the Supreme Court has rejected such efforts twice, adding: "Third time is not the charm." White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis called the decision "just another ruling from an activist judge" and said the order was consistent with the Supreme Court's analysis.

For scale, the Migration Policy Institute estimated last year that about 255,000 babies a year would have been denied citizenship under the original order. The fight sits within a wider immigration crackdown, including visa and asylum limits and lawsuits to strip citizenship from naturalised people who concealed major crimes.
a3c3fc2706d7.summary: A federal judge blocked Trump's narrower birthright citizenship order, ruling the president can't create new exceptions. It follows a June Supreme Court defeat; the White House called the ruling the work of an activist judge.
a3c3fc2706d7.why_it_matters: Citizenship rules shape the legal status of hundreds of thousands of births a year, with consequences for families, employers and public benefits. Repeated legal setbacks also signal how hard it is to change constitutional rights by executive order, which matters for planning around immigration policy.
key_points: Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the August orders on birthright citizenship.
The ruling follows a June Supreme Court decision striking down Trump's first order.
The White House called it an activist ruling; the ACLU said the law is settled.

25927c0f40db.headline: Is Alice Huang a Chinese spy? Nvidia's scandal rests on a claim nobody has proven
body: The biggest open question in the Nvidia scandal is whether Alice Huang, a former executive at data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was reinstated this Monday, according to TechCrunch.

The allegation began inside the U.S. government. It appeared in a classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump's May trip to China. Reports differ on what it said: the Wall Street Journal says it did not definitively call her a spy, while CNN says it concluded she was an intelligence asset.

What looks better established is contact. The New York Times, citing people familiar with U.S. intelligence reports, said she was in touch with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this fall, overlapping her relationship with Jensen Huang. Beijing calls the claims a smear, and Megaspeed says she left in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.

Since Trump pushed for Huang's return, top officials have largely walked the story back. Attorney General Todd Blanche said he had no reason to call Nvidia anything but a good corporate citizen, and senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress there is apparently no evidence the MSS directed her to pursue the affair. But as TechCrunch notes, not being told to have an affair is not the same as not being a spy.

Circumstantial details keep the doubts alive: Megaspeed was investigated over illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband is said to have close MSS ties. Rep. Jim Himes wondered whether she was a spy or a useful idiot, and the Journal noted that Chinese executives often keep ties to intelligence services without being formal assets.

The timing is the crux. Unless new intelligence has surfaced, and none has been made public, the reversal could reflect political pressure as easily as new facts. Jensen Huang is due before the Senate Banking Committee next week, though such hearings rarely reveal fresh secrets.
25927c0f40db.summary: The claim that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy remains unproven. U.S. officials have downplayed it since Nvidia's CEO was reinstated, leaving open whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure.
25927c0f40db.pixel_take: A spy thriller where the evidence is anonymous, the plot twist arrived right after the CEO's reinstatement, and the next scene is a Senate hearing. Don't expect the credits to explain much.
25927c0f40db.why_it_matters: Nvidia is central to the AI chip supply chain, so questions about its leadership and possible China links can shake investor confidence and policy decisions. Export controls and chip-smuggling scrutiny are already live issues, and political meddling in intelligence assessments adds uncertainty for markets.
key_points: Alice Huang's alleged spy role is unproven; reports on the classified memo conflict.
She reportedly was in contact with a Chinese MSS officer, but officials say no evidence shows the agency directed the affair.
Jensen Huang faces the Senate Banking Committee next week.

a2f8f08b11e4.headline: Trump's New Tariffs Put Asia's Trade Partners in a Familiar Squeeze Between Washington and Beijing
body: President Trump has signaled to trading partners across Asia that he is ready to escalate tariffs, according to The New York Times, bringing the spotlight back to the question of how hard Washington is willing to press China.

The message lands on a region with a tricky balancing act. Many Asian economies depend on trade and investment from both the United States and China, so a tariff fight between the two giants is less a spectator sport and more a game in which they are standing on the field.

The material available gives only the broad outline: the latest tariffs, the stated willingness to escalate, and the audience of Asian trading partners. Specific rates, product lists and start dates were not provided, so it is too early to size the direct hit to any one country.

Still, the logic of the signal is easy to follow. Tariffs aimed at pressuring China can ripple outward, because supply chains in Asia are deeply intertwined with Chinese factories and with American customers. Governments in the region may feel pushed to show where they stand, even though they would prefer to keep both relationships healthy.

For businesses and investors, the uncertainty is the story. Companies that source parts across borders tend to hold off on big decisions when trade rules keep shifting, and markets often react to the threat of escalation as much as to the tariffs themselves.
a2f8f08b11e4.summary: President Trump has told Asian trading partners he is ready to escalate tariffs, per The New York Times, renewing pressure on China and putting regional economies tied to both powers in a delicate spot.
a2f8f08b11e4.pixel_take: Asia's economies are being asked to pick a favorite parent at the dinner table, while both parents are also paying their rent.
a2f8f08b11e4.why_it_matters: Tariffs can raise costs for companies and consumers and disrupt supply chains that run through Asia. Investors tend to price in uncertainty quickly, so escalation threats can move markets even before new duties take effect.
key_points: Trump signaled readiness to escalate tariffs, per The New York Times.
Many Asian partners rely on trade and investment from both the US and China.
Details such as rates and timing were not provided in the available material.

8c1fc49ea098.headline: NVIDIA reportedly pauses AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries as US closes a loophole
body: NVIDIA has reportedly stopped allowing AI server hardware to be shipped to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to The Financial Times as relayed by Engadget. Manufacturing partners including Dell and Supermicro told clients in those countries that the chipmaker would not let their orders go out. The report says it is unclear whether the halt is temporary.

The timing is tied to a US crackdown. Chinese AI labs had been reaching NVIDIA's most powerful chips by renting computing power from cloud providers in these four countries, which bought servers with NVIDIA GPUs inside. That route sat in a gap in US export controls, and the Commerce Department has recently moved to close it with new rules aimed at exactly that practice.

On Wednesday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to its Entity List. Megaspeed had leased access to NVIDIA chips to Chinese companies. NVIDIA and others now need a US license to ship goods covered by export rules to the firm, and the Justice Department is reportedly investigating whether Megaspeed broke export rules.

The new rule gives data centers that already supply large amounts of computing power to China-based companies, or other covered locations, 90 days from November 19 to obtain a license. One cloud executive told the FT there is no guidance on how to apply while the clock ticks, calling the situation "sheer chaos in the region."

The story also has a boardroom subplot. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a former Megaspeed executive that some US officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset. NVIDIA reinstated him days ago, per Engadget.

The stakes are large. Chinese demand fueled a data center building boom across Southeast Asia, and NVIDIA booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, up 72 percent from the year before.
8c1fc49ea098.summary: NVIDIA has reportedly halted AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the US shuts a loophole letting Chinese firms rent its top chips, according to the Financial Times.
8c1fc49ea098.pixel_take: When your biggest regional customer is also the subject of a Justice Department probe, a shipping pause is the polite version of 'please hold.' Meanwhile, the license line has no front door.
8c1fc49ea098.why_it_matters: Southeast Asia has become a major hub for AI data centers and a big source of NVIDIA's revenue, so a prolonged halt could ripple through chip sales and server makers like Dell and Supermicro. It also shows how export rules can reshape supply chains and investor expectations almost overnight.
key_points: Dell and Supermicro reportedly told clients in four countries NVIDIA is blocking their server orders
US rules give affected data centers 90 days from November 19 to get a license
Megaspeed was added to the Entity List and is under Justice Department investigation

77af3ff41f51.headline: Paris appeals court sends Gérard Depardieu to trial over alleged 2018 rape of actress Charlotte Arnould
body: A Paris appeals court has ruled that French actor Gérard Depardieu, 77, must stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, according to BBC News. The ruling came on Thursday.

Arnould was 22 when, she says, the assault took place after she went to his Paris home to rehearse a play. She reported it several days later. She has waived her right to anonymity, and her lawyer, Carine Durrieu Diebolt, called the ruling a "first" and said the coming trial would be historic.

Depardieu had challenged his indictment on two counts of rape. The court upheld the case over the events of 7 August 2018, but he will not be tried over a second alleged rape at a hotel six days later. His lawyer, David-Olivier Kaminski, said the court had partly ruled in his client's favour and that the defence would consider an appeal to the Court of Cassation. In a 2023 letter in Le Figaro, Depardieu denied the allegations, saying there was never any coercion or violence between them.

The case was first dismissed for insufficient evidence. After Arnould filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation opened in the summer of 2020. Much of what happened at the house was reportedly captured on the actor's own CCTV.

The ruling lands amid other legal trouble. Last year Depardieu received an 18-month suspended sentence for sexually assaulting two women on a film set and was placed on the sex offenders register. He dropped his appeal last week and offered apologies. He is also under a separate investigation, alongside author Michel Houellebecq, over allegations linked to the 2018 film Thalasso, which French authorities confirmed last week.
77af3ff41f51.summary: A Paris appeals court has ordered Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for the alleged 2018 rape of actress Charlotte Arnould. He denies the claims, and his lawyer is weighing an appeal to the Court of Cassation.
77af3ff41f51.why_it_matters: The case shows how French courts are treating #MeToo-era allegations against major cultural figures, which can affect film financing, insurance and distribution decisions. Studios and producers face growing reputational and legal risk when working with people facing such accusations.
key_points: A Paris appeals court confirmed Depardieu will stand trial over the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould in 2018.
He will not be tried over a second alleged incident at a hotel six days later.
His lawyer is considering an appeal to the Court of Cassation; he denies the allegations.

719568056a2e.headline: Spain Wants Its Financial Watchdog to Hit the Freeze Button on Crypto Accounts
body: Spain is moving to give its financial intelligence unit the power to suspend crypto accounts, according to Cointelegraph. The plan would be set out in a new decree, and crypto firms that fail to comply would face fines.

The material available so far is thin. It does not say how the suspensions would work in practice, which triggers would allow them, or when the decree might take effect. Those details will matter a great deal once the text is public.

Still, the direction is clear. Financial intelligence units usually sit at the center of anti-money-laundering efforts, collecting and analyzing suspicious activity reports. Giving Spain's unit the ability to actually freeze crypto accounts would turn it from an observer that flags problems into an authority that can stop money in its tracks.

The fines are the other half of the story. Putting penalties on firms that ignore a suspension order pushes responsibility onto exchanges and other crypto service providers. In practice, that means compliance teams would need systems that can act quickly when an order lands.

For users, the open question is process: how long an account can stay frozen, what recourse exists, and how errors get fixed. Those safeguards usually decide whether a new power feels like targeted enforcement or a blunt instrument.
719568056a2e.summary: Spain plans a decree letting its financial intelligence unit suspend crypto accounts, with fines for firms that don't comply, according to Cointelegraph. Details on triggers and timing remain unclear.
719568056a2e.pixel_take: Spain's watchdog may soon get a freeze button for crypto accounts. Finally, something in crypto that responds instantly, though probably not the kind of speed holders were hoping for.
719568056a2e.why_it_matters: Tighter powers over crypto accounts raise compliance costs and legal risk for exchanges operating in Spain. For users, it is a reminder that holdings on regulated platforms can be frozen by authorities, which affects how much risk you take with custodial accounts.

569073855f68.headline: EU Leaders Haggle Over a $1.76 Trillion Budget and a $49bn Ukraine Loan, and Nobody Blinks
body: European Union leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday for an extraordinary summit and failed to quickly agree on the bloc's roughly $1.76 trillion budget proposal for 2028 to 2034, or on a new $49bn loan for Ukraine, according to Al Jazeera. The talks could stretch into Friday.

The room was split on basic philosophy. Some leaders want belts tightened, while others defend traditional spending policies that eat up large parts of the budget. Most, however, want extra money for new priorities and for Ukraine, almost five years into the war. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz summed up the contradiction: Europe cannot take on more debt, yet has tasks it must fulfil reliably.

Expectations were low from the start. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the sides were "light-years away from a solution" and that Italy will not sign a budget that gives more to receive less. Hungary's Peter Magyar wrote on Facebook that the chance of a deal on Thursday was virtually zero, and a Christmas agreement looked unlikely too. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said the budget must be modernised and downsized, and that he is ready for a marathon.

The stakes are high because the budget needs unanimous approval from all 27 members. Leaders want a deal by year-end since elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia could complicate talks. European Council President Antonio Costa urged an open mind and a sense of compromise.

Ukraine is a central piece. The proposal foresees $110bn for Kyiv over seven years, and leaders must also decide whether the cost of servicing the new loan should come from the budget. Merz has threatened to hold up a budget deal without a collective commitment to Ukraine from all members, while Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid.

The urgency comes from Kyiv's finances. A $99bn loan endorsed almost a year ago covers most of Ukraine's government needs for two years, but Russian attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure and disruptions to Black Sea trade are straining the budget.
569073855f68.summary: EU leaders struggled at a Brussels summit to agree a $1.76 trillion budget for 2028 to 2034 and a new $49bn Ukraine loan, with deep splits over spending, debt and military aid, Al Jazeera reports.
569073855f68.why_it_matters: The EU budget shapes funding for defence, the single market and Ukraine's finances, all of which influence European growth and borrowing. Prolonged deadlock could delay support for Kyiv and add political uncertainty ahead of a heavy election year.
key_points: EU leaders failed to quickly agree a roughly $1.76 trillion budget for 2028 to 2034 or a new $49bn Ukraine loan.
Unanimity among all 27 members is required, and leaders want a deal by year-end before 2026 elections complicate talks.
Merz wants a collective Ukraine commitment, while Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia oppose funding military aid.

9ab1d867793f.headline: X Adds Parental Controls After 20 Years, With a Twist: Teens Get a Say
body: X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has rolled out parental controls for teenage users, TechCrunch reported on November 26, 2026. The tools let parents and guardians manage what their kids see and do on the platform, arriving roughly two decades after the service launched.

Accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will default to "protected mode," according to the company. That means no sensitive content and no targeted ads. Unlike many rival systems, X lets teens see which restrictions have been applied to their accounts.

Parents get a fairly long menu of options. They can view weekly time spent on X, set daily limits, approve new followers, restrict feed recommendations and videos to accounts already followed, filter specific words, switch off sensitive media, choose who can DM their teen, and see who the teen is messaging.

There are limits to the oversight. Parents cannot read private messages, view search or viewing history, or post on their teen's behalf. Michael O'Herlihy, X's head of safety, wrote in a blog post that the aim is to balance parental guardrails with teens keeping ownership of their accounts.

The timing is awkward. TechCrunch notes the launch comes months after X was criticized over its AI chatbot being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The outlet also says the platform has long struggled with child sexual abuse material, misinformation and AI bots, and openly allows porn.

X has not traditionally targeted teens, but they are there anyway: a 2024 study found nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account, and the minimum age is 13. Whether the new tools meaningfully change the experience will depend on how many families actually switch them on.
9ab1d867793f.summary: X has launched parental controls for 13-to-17-year-olds, with protected mode by default and visibility for teens into restrictions. The rollout follows months of criticism over safety failures on the platform, TechCrunch reports.
9ab1d867793f.pixel_take: After 20 years, X has discovered the seatbelt. Better late than never, though the car has had some memorable moments without one.
9ab1d867793f.why_it_matters: Pressure on social platforms to protect minors keeps growing, and safety failures can bring regulatory, advertiser and legal risk. Default no-targeted-ads settings for teens also touch the ad business that funds platforms like X.
key_points: Teen accounts (13-17) default to protected mode: no sensitive content, no targeted ads.
Parents can set time limits, approve followers and control DMs but cannot read messages or see history.
Launch follows criticism over X's AI chatbot generating sexualized images and long-running content problems.

48e81f6caab2.headline: Bitcoin Clings to $60K While a Death Cross Crashes the Thanksgiving Table
body: Bitcoin and most major cryptocurrencies edged higher on Thursday as U.S. stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving, according to Decrypt. Bitcoin traded around $60,560 in the early afternoon Eastern time, up 1.39% over 24 hours but down 3.67% on the week.

The modest bounce follows a rough Wednesday. Bitcoin dipped to $57,500 and has since recovered roughly 5%. Ethereum gained 0.87% to just under $1,700, while XRP rose 3.1% and Solana 2.17%. The Nasdaq Composite had plunged as much as 4.6% on Wednesday before closing down 0.62%.

Decrypt links the selloff to stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, proposed tariffs and renewed worries about AI stocks. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index, rose 3.8% year over year in October, making it harder to bring inflation back to the 2% target.

The technical picture for Bitcoin looks bleak. Its 50-day exponential moving average has fallen below its 200-day, forming a bearish death cross. Bitcoin sits about 16% under the 50-day EMA of $71,478 and 19% under the 200-day EMA of $74,516, per TradingView charts cited by Decrypt.

The S&P 500 CFD, a derivative tracking the index, is still in golden cross territory, with its 50-day EMA above its 200-day. But the price is below both and the gap is narrowing, which hints that the bullish trend is losing steam. Neither signal guarantees what comes next.

Traders now eye resistance between $62,000 and $64,000, with support around $57,500 to $58,500 and November's low near $55,000. About $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire Friday on Deribit, with traders leaning more toward downside protection than in October. U.S. stocks reopen Friday, with the NYSE closing early at 1 p.m. ET.
48e81f6caab2.summary: Bitcoin ticked up to about $60,560 as U.S. markets closed for Thanksgiving, but a death cross and sticky 3.8% inflation show crypto is hurting more than stocks.
48e81f6caab2.pixel_take: Bitcoin spent Thanksgiving trying to digest a death cross, which is a lot to ask after a day when even the Nasdaq lost its appetite.
48e81f6caab2.why_it_matters: Sticky inflation and tariff worries can keep rate cuts off the table, which tends to pressure risk assets like crypto. Bitcoin's deeper technical damage versus stocks suggests investors are more cautious on it. Big options expiry could add volatility.
key_points: Bitcoin trades near $60,560, up 1.39% in 24 hours but down 3.67% on the week.
A death cross has formed, with price about 16% below its 50-day EMA.
About $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire Friday on Deribit.

6f444221f193.headline: Hating Nvidia's Jensen Huang while loving your 401(k) gains? MarketWatch asks if that makes you a hypocrite
body: MarketWatch published a reader-style question on November 26, 2026, that many retirement savers may quietly recognize: can you dislike that Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia while enjoying what the company has done for your 401(k)? The writer asks, with some self-awareness, whether that makes them a hypocrite.

The material available to us is thin: just the headline and a one-line teaser, with no full article text. The teaser offers the closest thing to an answer, saying that doing nothing and keeping an even temperament is often the work of gods. In other words, the advice seems to lean toward calm rather than guilt.

That hint fits a well-established idea in personal finance. Most 401(k) investors hold diversified funds, often index funds or target-date funds, so they own big companies like Nvidia without ever choosing them. Their gains are a side effect of a long-term plan, not a vote of approval for any one executive or corporate decision.

There is also a practical point. Reacting emotionally to a single company, whether by cheering or by selling out of annoyance, tends to be a poor way to manage retirement money. Steady contributions and patience are the usual recommendation, which is presumably what the teaser's nod to temperament is getting at.

We can't say more about the specifics of the writer's complaint, since the source text is not available. What the headline does capture is a familiar tension of modern investing: your portfolio does not need to share your opinions.
6f444221f193.summary: A MarketWatch question asks whether it's hypocritical to dislike Jensen Huang's return at Nvidia while enjoying the 401(k) gains. The teaser suggests staying calm and doing nothing.
6f444221f193.pixel_take: Your 401(k) doesn't care about your feelings, which is honestly its best quality. Think of it as the one employee who works well with people you can't stand.
6f444221f193.why_it_matters: Many people's retirement savings are tied to big tech names through index and target-date funds, so strong gains can feel personal. The story is a reminder that emotional reactions to one company or executive rarely make a good investment strategy.

The teaser suggests an even temperament and doing nothing is the wise approach.

bf342bcea039.headline: Zodia Custody Admits Hackers Peeked at Client Contact Details, But Says Funds Are Safe
body: Zodia Custody, the crypto custodian backed by Standard Chartered, has disclosed that an unauthorized party gained access to some client and staff names and email addresses, according to Decrypt. The firm said it found no unauthorized transactions.

Based on the information available, the exposed data appears limited to contact details rather than the assets the company safeguards. That is a meaningful distinction for a business whose entire pitch is keeping other people's digital money locked down.

Still, a custodian is not a place you want uninvited guests, even ones who only browse the guest list. Names and email addresses may look harmless, but in crypto they can be raw material for phishing, where scammers pose as a trusted provider and nudge people into handing over credentials or approving shady transfers.

The report does not include further detail, such as how the intruder got in, how many people were affected, or when the access happened. Those answers will matter for judging how serious the incident really is and how well the company's defenses held up.

Custodians like Zodia serve institutional clients who want the security and compliance of a bank-linked provider rather than leaving coins on an exchange or in a personal wallet. For that audience, trust is the product, so how the firm communicates and follows up on this episode will be watched closely.
bf342bcea039.summary: Standard Chartered-backed Zodia Custody says an unauthorized party accessed some client and staff names and emails. The firm found no unauthorized transactions, according to Decrypt.
bf342bcea039.pixel_take: Hackers reportedly got the guest list but not the vault. Still, nobody wants a stranger reading the party invitations before the phishing emails go out.
bf342bcea039.why_it_matters: Custodians sell trust, so even a contact-data leak without stolen funds can dent confidence among institutional clients. Exposed emails can fuel targeted phishing, which is a real risk for anyone holding crypto. It is also a reminder that bank-linked branding doesn't make crypto infrastructure immune to breaches.
key_points: An unauthorized party accessed some client and staff names and emails at Zodia Custody.
The firm says it found no unauthorized transactions.
