0197668f1d5f.headline: Old TV Shows Are Having a Boom While New Ones Struggle for Attention
body: Viewers are retreating to the past. According to The New York Times, older television shows are enjoying a boom while new series are having a much tougher time finding an audience.

The Times points to three forces behind the shift: fewer original series being made, decision fatigue among viewers and a craving for comfort. In plain terms, there is less new stuff, choosing among it is exhausting, and a familiar show feels like a warm blanket.

Decision fatigue is a familiar problem in the streaming age. When a menu offers endless options, picking something can feel like work, and a show you already know is a safe bet that needs no research and no commitment.

The supply side matters too. With fewer original series being produced, the pool of fresh programming is shrinking just as old favorites remain easy to find. That tilts the playing field toward the back catalog.

The material available here is limited to the headline and teaser, so specific viewership figures, titles and platforms are not covered. The broader picture, though, is of audiences choosing comfort over novelty.

39a447c01990.headline: Ethereum Picks December 15 for Glamsterdam Testnet Fork After October Security Scare Hit the Brakes
body: Ethereum's core developers have set December 15 as the date for the delayed Glamsterdam testnet upgrade, according to Decrypt. The move follows a pause in October, when security concerns halted the fork on the Hoodi test network.

The headline detail is that the contested gas changes at the heart of Glamsterdam will ship unaltered, per Decrypt. In other words, developers are not rewriting that part of the upgrade to settle the dispute. They are going ahead with it as designed.

Gas is the fee mechanism that prices computation on Ethereum, so any change to how it works draws close scrutiny. Tweaks that look tidy on paper can have knock-on effects for how applications behave and how the network resists abuse. That helps explain why a security concern was enough to stop a test deployment in its tracks.

Testnets exist for exactly this kind of moment. Upgrades are rehearsed on networks where mistakes cost nothing before they reach the main Ethereum network, where real money is at stake. A paused fork on a testnet is the process working, not breaking, even if it is less fun to tweet about.

The material available to us does not say when Glamsterdam could reach mainnet, nor does it detail the specific security concerns. Those answers will likely depend on how the December 15 test goes. For now, the date gives the ecosystem a concrete checkpoint after weeks of uncertainty.
39a447c01990.summary: Ethereum developers have scheduled the delayed Glamsterdam testnet upgrade for December 15, Decrypt reports, keeping the contested gas changes intact after security concerns stopped the Hoodi fork in October.
39a447c01990.pixel_take: Ethereum's developers hit pause, argued about gas, and are now pressing go anyway. Software engineering's version of 'we've talked about it, and the plan stays the plan.'

341a3dede6b5.headline: Tidal Bans Fully AI-Made Songs, Plans to Purge 29 Million Tracks From Its Catalog
body: Streaming service Tidal says it will ban fully AI-generated songs starting December 9, and will delete an estimated 29 million of them, according to Futurism. Robert Andersen, Tidal's head at parent company Block, announced the policy in a statement on X.

Andersen said the ban should stop as many as 85,000 machine-made tracks a day from flooding the platform. He argued the move would resonate with artists and listeners, noting that 96 percent of all AI-generated songs get zero plays.

Tidal's own numbers explain the urgency. Over the past 90 days, more than 43 percent of tracks submitted to the service were fully AI-generated. Left in place, they would have eaten into the revenue pool that pays real musicians. The company also said wholly AI-generated music meant to mislead listeners and impersonate artists diverts streams and royalties and confuses fans.

Futurism reports this makes Tidal the only major streaming platform with a wholesale ban on fully AI-generated songs. It follows a summer policy of scanning for tracks its systems judged 100 percent AI-generated, labelling them and demonetizing them.

Rivals have taken softer routes. Spotify said last month it pulled more than 50 million songs it deemed AI spam out of its recommendation algorithms, but did not delete them. It has also resisted AI labels, which YouTube Music uses, and is reportedly preparing an AI remixing feature. Bandcamp also bans such music, though Futurism notes it is a distribution platform rather than a full streamer.
The split shows how streamers are choosing between treating AI music as spam to be managed and treating it as a line to be drawn.
341a3dede6b5.summary: Tidal will ban fully AI-generated songs from December 9 and remove an estimated 29 million tracks, saying they crowd out human artists and divert royalties. Rivals like Spotify have chosen softer measures.
341a3dede6b5.pixel_take: Tidal just told 29 million robot songs their time is up. Given that 96 percent of them had no listeners, the farewell party will be a very quiet one.
341a3dede6b5.why_it_matters: Streaming royalties come from a shared pool, so every AI track that draws plays shrinks the payout to human artists. How platforms handle AI content could shape music revenue, listener trust and competition among streamers.
key_points: Tidal bans fully AI-generated songs from December 9 and plans to delete about 29 million tracks.
Over 43 percent of tracks submitted in the past 90 days were fully AI-generated, per Tidal.
Spotify only removed AI spam from recommendations and is reportedly preparing an AI remix feature.

53354c5781ee.headline: The Com: Cybercrime Network Called a 'Chilling Threat' to Children
body: The Com, short for "the Community," is a global cybercrime network that crime agencies around the world are warning about, according to The Guardian. The name sounds like a book club or a neighborhood association. Authorities say it is nothing of the kind.

The FBI estimates that thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of the group, The Guardian reports. The network is linked to the creation and sharing of indecent images of girls, as well as to blackmail.

The material available for this report is limited to the headline and teaser of The Guardian's piece, so details on how the network operates, where its members are based and what enforcement action has been taken are not covered here. What is clear is the scale of concern: agencies across several countries are sounding the alarm, and the language used about the threat to children is stark.

Cases like this show how online crime has changed. Loosely organized networks can form across borders and recruit through ordinary internet platforms. This makes them hard for any single national police force to track, and it is why international cooperation between agencies matters so much.

Parents, schools and technology companies are all part of the picture. Platforms face growing pressure to detect abusive material and to protect young users, while families are urged to talk openly with children about online contact and pressure. Anyone worried about a child being targeted should contact local law enforcement.
53354c5781ee.summary: The FBI estimates thousands of people identify as current or recent members of the Com, a global network linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail, according to The Guardian. Agencies worldwide are warning about it.
53354c5781ee.why_it_matters: Cross-border online crime networks put pressure on technology platforms, regulators and police budgets, and can raise compliance costs for companies that host user content. For families, it is a reminder that online safety is a real, practical concern.
key_points: The FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members or recent members of the Com.
The network is linked to indecent images of girls and to blackmail.
Crime agencies around the world are warning about the threat, per The Guardian.

12e3ae11c270.headline: Democrats vs. Trump: Federal Contractors May Get Squeezed in the Middle
body: Incoming Democratic majorities have started aiming their planned investigations at businesses and other outside parties, according to The New York Times. The catch: President Trump has threatened to fire those that cooperate without his permission.

That sets up an awkward standoff for companies that do business with the federal government. One side holds subpoena-style leverage over information, the other holds the contracts. Based on the Times' account, firms could be caught between the two.

The material available is limited, so details are thin on which companies are being targeted, what Democrats are seeking, or how Trump's threat would be carried out. What is clear is the basic dynamic: Congress wants cooperation from outsiders, and the White House is warning that cooperating on its own terms could cost them their work.

For contractors, this is a classic no-win scenario. Ignoring a congressional inquiry can carry its own risks, while angering the biggest customer in the country is not a comfortable alternative. Legal teams will likely spend a lot of time weighing which door is less painful.

Oversight fights between Congress and a president of the opposing party are nothing new. But pulling private companies into the middle, with the threat of losing federal business, raises the stakes for businesses that usually prefer to stay out of political crossfire.
12e3ae11c270.summary: Incoming Democratic majorities are targeting businesses in planned inquiries, while Trump threatens to fire contractors who comply without his permission, per The New York Times. Companies face pressure from both sides.
12e3ae11c270.pixel_take: Federal contractors are about to learn what the middle seat feels like: Congress wants answers, the White House wants silence, and everyone wants to keep the paycheck.
12e3ae11c270.why_it_matters: Federal contracts are a major revenue source for many companies, so political threats against them can affect earnings and stock performance. Businesses may face higher legal costs and uncertainty as oversight battles heat up.
key_points: Incoming Democratic majorities plan inquiries that reach businesses and other outsiders.
Trump has threatened to fire those who comply without his permission.
Federal contractors risk being squeezed between Congress and the White House.

377df4bfa50c.headline: Binance Reopens All Withdrawals Four Weeks After Record $6.4B Hack
body: Binance said on Thursday that it has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it imposed after the record $6.4 billion hack of the exchange on October 29, roughly four weeks after the attack, according to Decrypt.

The exchange said its recovery work is complete and withdrawals are open across nearly all networks. A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance or planned upgrades, which Binance described as routine and separate from the hack. It also said user assets remain fully backed and pointed customers to its proof-of-reserves page, which it says shows holdings backed at least 1:1.

Binance also warned of phishing. It said it will never ask for passwords, two-factor codes or seed phrases, and will never reach out to offer to speed up withdrawals, give priority processing or move assets into a so-called Binance vault.

On the investigation side, the FBI has attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, which Pyongyang denies. Binance set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses and won a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts. On Monday the U.S. Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture action for more than $1.1 billion in USDC and said the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion since the attack.

The hackers are still moving funds. Chainalysis and Elliptic estimates, cited by Reuters, show more than $600 million passed through cross-chain exchange THORChain, while Elliptic says $342 million went through a Bitcoin coinjoin service, up from $247 million earlier in the week. TRM Labs' Ari Redbord told Reuters that laundering could take months or years, but cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea.

THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford defended the protocol, saying by his count 98% of its volume is legitimate trading and that shutting it down would hurt ordinary users while barely slowing the hackers. TRM Labs estimates THORChain may have earned as much as $1 million in fees from the launderers' swaps.
377df4bfa50c.summary: Binance has restored withdrawals four weeks after the $6.4 billion October hack, while U.S. authorities say $2.9 billion has been frozen, seized or returned and hackers keep laundering funds through THORChain and coinjoin services.
377df4bfa50c.pixel_take: Binance has reopened the doors and promised the vault is full. Meanwhile the thieves are still trying to launder the loot, and a decentralized protocol insists it's just the world's busiest, most awkward bystander.
377df4bfa50c.why_it_matters: Restored withdrawals and proof-of-reserves claims go a long way toward calming users after the largest exchange hack on record. The case also keeps the pressure on decentralized services like THORChain, a debate that shapes crypto regulation and how safe it is to keep money on exchanges.
key_points: Binance fully lifted its post-hack withdrawal suspension, with a few networks paused for routine maintenance.
The U.S. says it has helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion, and filed a forfeiture action for more than $1.1 billion in USDC.
Hackers continue laundering funds via THORChain and a Bitcoin coinjoin service, per Chainalysis and Elliptic estimates.

17214fd653db.headline: Akai stops fighting MPC Sample modders and hands them the keys with firmware 1.4
body: Akai has released MPC Sample 1.4, a firmware update that officially opens its compact, budget-friendly sampler to modders and third-party developers, according to The Verge. The company says it chose to embrace a growing community of tinkerers rather than fight it.

The device had already become a popular playground for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods, meaning add-ons built with heavy help from AI coding tools. Version 1.4 adds support for a new SDK and for custom Knob Effects plugins. Drop a plugin into the right folder on the microSD card and it shows up at the bottom of the Knob Effects menu automatically.

A new Developer Mode lets users run scripts from the microSD card or reach the sampler's internal filesystem over USB. There is also remote screen access, so the display can be mirrored on an external monitor using the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.

Not everything is for coders. A flatten pad feature speeds up resampling when you want to bake effects into individual pads, and sequence record autoplay gives the machine a looper-like feel. The 16-levels pad mode also gets a scale option, so you can play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major or whichever key your track lives in, instead of being stuck with 16 chromatic notes.
The Verge notes this is part of Akai's wider push to open up its music-making platforms. For a tour of the custom firmwares and effects already out there, the outlet points to a video from Loopop.
17214fd653db.summary: Akai's MPC Sample 1.4 firmware officially opens the affordable sampler to modders with an SDK, custom effect plugins and a Developer Mode, plus new features like scale-aware pads, per The Verge.
17214fd653db.pixel_take: Akai looked at the hobbyists hacking its gear and chose the classic move: if you can't beat them, give them an SDK. Somewhere, a vibe-coded reverb is already feeling very validated.
17214fd653db.why_it_matters: Hardware makers are discovering that an engaged modding community can add value without extra engineering cost. Opening a cheap device to third-party code can extend its useful life and make it more attractive to buyers who want something that keeps improving.
key_points: MPC Sample 1.4 adds an SDK, custom Knob Effects plugins and a Developer Mode.
Plugins load from the microSD card; the filesystem is reachable over USB and the screen can be mirrored.
New pad features include flatten pad, sequence record autoplay and scale options for 16-levels mode.

336da795fdb3.headline: Two New TV Shows Take On Sam Bankman-Fried and the FTX Collapse, With Different Angles
body: Two screen projects are revisiting the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the crypto exchange FTX, according to The New York Times: a limited series called "The Altruists" and a documentary titled "The Boy Who Stole Billions?"

The Times says the two productions take different approaches to the founder's role in what it describes as one of the largest frauds in history. The material available does not detail those differences, so we won't guess at plot points, casting or how each one portrays him.

The pairing does say something about the format wars of modern entertainment. A scripted series can dramatize what happened behind closed doors, while a documentary leans on real footage and testimony. Note the question mark in the documentary's title, which hints at a debate over how the story should be framed.

Financial scandals have become reliable television material. They have money, ambition, big personalities and a dramatic fall, and viewers who never read a balance sheet will happily watch one explode on screen.

For the crypto industry, the timing is a reminder that the FTX saga remains a reference point. Whenever regulators, investors or lawmakers discuss exchange oversight, custody of customer funds or trust in digital assets, the collapse is still the cautionary tale people reach for.
336da795fdb3.summary: The New York Times reviews two new TV takes on Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX: the limited series "The Altruists" and the documentary "The Boy Who Stole Billions?", which differ on his role in the fraud.
336da795fdb3.pixel_take: Two shows, one fraud, zero need for a spoiler alert. The only thing more reliable than crypto volatility is Hollywood's appetite for a spectacular financial faceplant.
336da795fdb3.why_it_matters: Popular retellings shape how the public remembers the FTX collapse, and that memory influences trust in crypto exchanges and the appetite for regulation. For anyone holding digital assets, the story remains a lesson about where your money actually sits.
key_points: The Times covers a limited series, "The Altruists," and a documentary, "The Boy Who Stole Billions?"
Both examine Sam Bankman-Fried's role in the FTX fraud, but from different angles.
The Times calls the FTX collapse one of the largest frauds in history.

1cbb0f1fc539.headline: Alexander the Great's tomb hunt gets a lead as Egypt unearths a monumental burial complex
body: Archaeologists in Egypt have uncovered a monumental structure in the Royal Quarter of ancient Alexandria that is believed to be a burial complex, raising hopes of progress in one of archaeology's longest-running mysteries, according to Metro. The mystery is where Alexander the Great was laid to rest.

Alexander, whose empire spanned three continents, died in 323 BCE and was first buried in Memphis. His body was later moved to Alexandria, one of the cities named after him. Mentions of the tomb vanish from records by the 4th or 5th century, and experts think it was damaged or buried by natural disaster or civic upheaval.

The newly found remains include large stone structures surrounded by walls, plus a tunnel running beneath the building toward the north. Researchers have not conclusively established what the building is, but its location, monumental scale and architectural features point to a tomb. Historical accounts suggest such a complex held the remains of Ptolemaic rulers, and the possibility that Alexander himself lies there has not been ruled out.

A specialist scientific committee has been appointed to study the find. Part of its work will be comparing the site with the topographical map of ancient Alexandria and tracing the full extent of the foundations. Dr Hisham Al-Lithi of Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said the initial assessment confirmed the discovery's importance, particularly because of its place in the Royal Quarter. He added that further archaeological and architectural work is needed to pin down the buildings' function and their relationship to nearby sites.

The ancient sources give the hunt some footing. The Greek writer Zenobius noted that Ptolemy IV Philopator built a funerary monument for his ancestors, including Alexander, and the geographer Strabo also described the burial complex. Searches have gone on since the 19th century, with Greek and Egyptian teams stepping up efforts over the past two decades at the Shallalat Gardens site, where this latest structure was found.
1cbb0f1fc539.summary: Archaeologists in Alexandria, Egypt, found a monumental structure in the Royal Quarter believed to be a tomb. Its identity is unconfirmed, but it revives hopes of finding Alexander the Great's long-lost burial place.
1cbb0f1fc539.pixel_take: After roughly 1,700 years of the world's most patient game of hide-and-seek, archaeologists may have found a promising hallway. Alexander, as ever, is taking his time.
1cbb0f1fc539.why_it_matters: Major finds like this can boost cultural tourism and global attention for Egypt, a sector that matters to its economy. They also show how slow, committee-driven research can turn a legend into a verifiable site, which is something heritage investors and visitors both watch closely.
key_points: A monumental, probably tomb-like structure was found in Alexandria's Royal Quarter.
Its identity is unconfirmed; a scientific committee will study it, including whether Alexander could be linked.
The site sits within the Shallalat Gardens area, long searched by Greek and Egyptian teams.

190a20f2d9bd.headline: Hamas Leader Khalil al-Hayya's Last Surviving Son Survives Israeli Strike in Gaza
body: Izzeldeen, the last surviving son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, survived an Israeli assassination attempt in Gaza on Friday, according to Al Jazeera, which cited senior Hamas official Basem Naim.
Al Jazeera reported that four of Izzeldeen's brothers have been killed by Israeli forces. They include his twin, Hamam, who died in a 2025 airstrike in Qatar.

The material available so far is thin. It does not say where in Gaza the strike took place, how it was carried out, or whether anyone else was hurt. It also contains no Israeli response. The account of the attempt rests on the statement from a Hamas official as relayed by Al Jazeera.

The episode shows that targeted strikes on Hamas leaders and their families continue to be a feature of the conflict. The reference to a 2025 strike in Qatar is a reminder that such operations have reached beyond Gaza's borders and drawn in third countries.
190a20f2d9bd.summary: Hamas official Basem Naim said Izzeldeen, the last surviving son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, survived an Israeli assassination attempt in Gaza on Friday, according to Al Jazeera.
190a20f2d9bd.why_it_matters: Strikes on senior militants and their families can complicate ceasefire diplomacy and mediation efforts. That raises regional risk, which tends to affect energy prices, investor sentiment and the outlook for reconstruction funding.
key_points: Izzeldeen al-Hayya survived an Israeli assassination attempt in Gaza on Friday, per Hamas official Basem Naim.
Four of his brothers have been killed by Israeli forces, including twin Hamam in a 2025 Qatar strike.

41209e3c7e99.headline: Nvidia whiplash puts Fed chief Warsh's love of market signals to the test
body: A week of wild market swings and drama around Nvidia has exposed a tension in how Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh wants to run policy, according to CNBC's Steve Liesman. Warsh favors market indicators over official forecasts, but the market's mood changed sharply from Friday to Monday.

On Friday, stocks sold off and market-implied odds of a Fed rate hike fell. By Monday, with Nvidia's Jensen Huang back in office, a strong rally restored expectations of two more hikes. CNBC notes the Goldman Sachs Financial Conditions Index eased by 22 basis points, reversing nearly half of the prior week's tightening, and both December and January hikes were back on the table.

Warsh's public message is to look past short-term volatility. He spent three hours in San Francisco presiding over a conference on AI and its economic effects, part of an AI task force that is one of five studying areas of Fed policymaking. He described the groups as a way to go deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves.

He has also trimmed post-meeting press conferences to half an hour and generally avoids forward guidance, so he spends much of the time fending off questions about the next move. CNBC likens his approach to his earlier work at Duquesne Family Office, where he judged early-stage tech bets on long-term payoffs even when the daily profit and loss looked ugly.

AI makes the dilemma sharper. Warsh has acknowledged the outlook is fast-moving and deeply uncertain. He showed particular interest in a possible 'China Shock' for U.S. service jobs, which could push rates lower over time, while the AI buildout currently looks inflationary and pushes rates higher. One development, two opposing signals.

Because policy works with long and variable lags, the Fed has to set rates for where the economy will be next year. Forecasts carry wide error bands, but so does market pricing. The open question, per CNBC, is which signals deserve attention and how long they must persist before they guide policy.
41209e3c7e99.summary: CNBC reports that a week of Nvidia-driven market swings highlights Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's dilemma: he wants to rely on market signals over forecasts, yet those signals flipped within days, with rate hike odds swinging back.
41209e3c7e99.pixel_take: Warsh wants to listen to the market, but this week the market changed its mind faster than a group chat picking a restaurant.
41209e3c7e99.why_it_matters: Fed rate decisions drive mortgage costs, savings yields and stock valuations. If the central bank leans on market signals that reverse in days, rate expectations could stay jumpy. AI spending is now a key force on both growth and inflation.
key_points: Rate-hike odds fell Friday, then recovered Monday as stocks rallied, with December and January hikes back on the table.
Warsh prefers market indicators to forecasts and avoids forward guidance, while stressing long-term thinking.
AI could be inflationary now yet cut jobs later, sending mixed signals for rates.

5648d4b4387f.headline: Anker's 100W universal travel charger hits $60, its lowest price yet, for Black Friday
body: Anker's 100W Universal Charger is on sale for $59.99 at Amazon, Best Buy and Walmart for Black Friday, according to The Verge. That is $20 off the list price and a few dollars below the previous best deal.
Both the dark gray and silver versions are discounted at all three retailers, so shoppers can pick a color without hunting for the best price.

The charger has four ports: three USB-C and one USB-A. It can power up to four devices at once, and two of the USB-C ports can deliver up to 100W when used individually. A small LCD screen shows how much power is flowing to your gadgets.

It fits outlets in more than 200 countries, including Type A (US, Canada, Japan, China), Type C (European Union) and Type G (UK, Singapore). The catch: it does not support Type I, used in Australia, New Zealand and Argentina.
It is also USB-only. There is no AC outlet, so anything that needs a traditional plug will need a separate solution. The Verge notes it may earn a commission from purchases made through its links.
5648d4b4387f.summary: Anker's 100W Universal Charger drops to $59.99 at Amazon, Best Buy and Walmart for Black Friday, $20 off and its lowest price yet, according to The Verge. It has four USB ports but no AC outlet.
5648d4b4387f.pixel_take: One charger, four ports, 200-plus countries, and a tiny screen to watch your power flow. Sadly, it still can't charge the Australian outlet problem away.
5648d4b4387f.why_it_matters: Travel gear is a classic Black Friday buy, and a 25% cut on a multi-device charger can replace several bulky adapters. As more laptops and phones charge over USB-C, one 100W port can do the work of several chargers.
key_points: The Anker 100W Universal Charger costs $59.99, $20 off, at Amazon, Best Buy and Walmart.
It has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, with up to 100W on two USB-C ports used individually.

4b2c934570ff.headline: Banned Nvidia Blackwell Racks Reportedly Surface in Shanghai as Trump Floats a U.S. Stake in the Chipmaker
body: Banned Nvidia hardware has reportedly turned up in China, and the politics around the company just got stranger. According to Decrypt, Nvidia racks that are barred from the Chinese market were found at a Shanghai data center tied to a person named Alice Huang.

The same report says President Donald Trump stated that the U.S. government could still take a stake in Nvidia. The material available gives no further detail on how such a stake would be structured, what it would cost, or whether any formal plan exists.

The source text was not available to us beyond the headline and teaser, so several questions remain open. We do not know how the racks reached Shanghai, who operated the data center, or whether Nvidia, U.S. officials or Chinese authorities have responded. Alice Huang's exact role has not been spelled out in the material we have.

Some context helps. Washington has restricted exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, and the Blackwell line is among the products caught up in that debate. Reports of restricted hardware appearing in Chinese facilities tend to raise familiar questions about enforcement, resale channels and how tightly export rules can really be policed.

The stake comment adds another layer. A government shareholding in a leading chipmaker would be an unusual step for the U.S., and even a casual mention can move sentiment among investors who watch Nvidia as a bellwether for the AI boom. For now it is a floated idea, not a policy, and this report does not say otherwise.
4b2c934570ff.summary: Decrypt reports banned Nvidia racks were found at a Shanghai data center tied to Alice Huang, while Trump said the U.S. could still take a stake in the chipmaker. Details remain thin.
4b2c934570ff.pixel_take: Banned chips apparently found a way through the border, while the president muses about becoming a shareholder. Export controls meet the world's most ambitious stock tip.
4b2c934570ff.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a bellwether for AI and for many investors' portfolios, so export enforcement and talk of government ownership can move sentiment. Chip rules also shape who gets access to cutting-edge computing, which affects the pace of AI development and the costs tied to it.
key_points: Decrypt reports banned Nvidia racks were found at a Shanghai data center tied to Alice Huang.
Trump said the U.S. could still take a stake in Nvidia.
Details on how the hardware got there and on any stake plan are not yet available.

ee58621c551c.headline: Rafael's high-energy laser zaps drones in joint US-Israel trials, new footage shows
body: Israeli defense contractor Rafael Advanced Defense Systems has released new footage of its high-energy laser in action during joint trials with the United States involving drones, according to Interesting Engineering.

The material available to us is thin: the headline and teaser describe the footage and the joint US-Israel setting, but no details on the tests, such as power levels, ranges, number of targets or results, were provided. We are not going to invent them, so treat this as a first look rather than a full technical report.

What we can say is why the topic keeps coming up. Cheap drones have become a headache for militaries because defending against them with conventional missiles can mean spending far more on the interceptor than the target is worth. Directed-energy weapons such as lasers are pitched as an answer, since each shot costs relatively little and the magazine, in theory, lasts as long as the power supply does.

Lasers are not magic, though. They are generally understood to be affected by weather and atmospheric conditions, and they need time on target to do their work. That is why defense planners tend to see them as one layer in a broader air-defense system rather than a replacement for missiles.

The joint nature of the trials also matters. Public demonstrations by a defense contractor serve a double purpose: they show progress to partner governments and signal to potential customers that the technology is maturing. Whether this footage leads to orders is something only future announcements will reveal.
ee58621c551c.summary: Rafael Advanced Defense Systems released new footage of its high-energy laser during joint US-Israel drone trials, per Interesting Engineering. Test details were not provided.
ee58621c551c.why_it_matters: Cheap drones are forcing militaries to rethink the economics of air defense, and lasers promise a lower cost per shot than missiles. Successful trials could shape defense budgets and boost the market for directed-energy technology.
key_points: Rafael released new footage of its high-energy laser in drone trials.
The trials were joint between the US and Israel.
Technical results were not detailed in the available material.
